cases.title: One City, Many Climates
cases.audience: General urban readers and community meeting attendees
cases.use_context: Opening spread of the special, viewed on a desktop/tablet or printed as a landscape editorial page
cases.user_goal: Recognize that heat varies both between a city and its surroundings and between blocks inside the city.

content_basis.verified_content: Heat-island definition and EPA U.S. daytime/nighttime urban-rural difference ranges
content_basis.interpretation: The visual contrast between regional and block scales is an editorial explanation, not a map of a real city.
content_basis.demonstration: Abstract city field and contour bands are conceptual; no place names or local measurements.

cases.visual_intent: An aerial abstract city field crossed by two nested contour systems; a crisp range-band inset establishes the difference between regional and intra-urban scale without implying local data.

criteria.condition: The regional contrast and within-city contrast are visibly distinct and labelled.
criteria.method: Open final PNG at full size and 50%; compare the two scale labels with the contour composition.

criteria.condition: The two EPA ranges appear exactly as about 1–7°F by day and about 2–5°F at night, with a U.S. source-review qualifier and no midpoint.
criteria.method: Read the rendered labels and compare with B04-D01 in the ledger.

criteria.condition: No contour, colour, or block is presented as a measured neighborhood value.
criteria.method: Check on-artwork note, case metadata, and absence of numeric locality labels.

criteria.condition: Title, subtitle, legend, and source note remain readable with no clipped text or contour collisions.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG, text-region crops, and edge bounds at target size.

cases.title: The Day's Heat Budget
cases.audience: Readers who think heat comes only from sunshine or air conditioners
cases.use_context: Explainer graphic in the special, landscape desktop reading
cases.user_goal: Explain how materials, missing vegetation, urban geometry, human activity, and weather jointly shape urban heat.

content_basis.verified_content: EPA lists reduced natural landscapes, material properties, urban geometry, anthropogenic heat, and weather/geography as contributing factors.
content_basis.interpretation: The phrase 'heat budget' is an editorial metaphor for interacting inputs and pathways.
content_basis.demonstration: Arrow widths and icon placement are conceptual; they are not energy quantities.

cases.visual_intent: A radial energy-flow board with a dark urban mass at the centre and five labelled pathways; bold arrows and material samples prevent a generic list-of-cards treatment.

criteria.condition: All five contributing factors are present and traceable to the source.
criteria.method: Count labels and cross-check B04-C03.

criteria.condition: The graphic states that arrow width is conceptual and does not encode measured energy shares.
criteria.method: Inspect the visible note and legend.

criteria.condition: Pathways do not overlap labels, arrows terminate cleanly, and rotated text remains legible.
criteria.method: Review full PNG and crops around each pathway endpoint.

criteria.condition: The composition reads as one interacting system rather than five unrelated facts.
criteria.method: At 50% view, verify the central mass visibly connects every pathway.

cases.title: Two Temperatures, Two Questions
cases.audience: Residents interpreting sidewalk thermometers, thermal maps, or weather reports
cases.use_context: Vertical mobile/tablet explainer within the special
cases.user_goal: Distinguish surface temperature from air temperature and understand why one cannot be substituted for the other.

content_basis.verified_content: Surface and atmospheric heat islands differ; surface values vary more during the day; air and surface observations have different uses and limitations.
content_basis.interpretation: A split thermometer composition visualises two measurement questions rather than a numerical conversion.
content_basis.demonstration: No invented temperature values or conversion formula.

cases.visual_intent: A tall split-field comparison: glowing pavement plane above, calm head-height air band below, with a dashed line that stops rather than implying equivalence.

criteria.condition: Surface and air are separately labelled with distinct observation locations and uses.
criteria.method: Inspect upper and lower panels and compare with B04-C04.

criteria.condition: No arrow, equation, or wording claims a fixed surface-to-air conversion.
criteria.method: Search the DSL text for conversion language and visually inspect the dashed divider.

criteria.condition: Both panels remain readable on a narrow portrait page without horizontal scrolling or tiny footnotes.
criteria.method: Review fit-height PNG and full-size crops of all body text.

criteria.condition: The split composition preserves enough whitespace to avoid confusing pavement heat with ambient air.
criteria.method: Inspect final PNG at target size and a 50% thumbnail.

cases.title: The Street Decides
cases.audience: Residents, designers, and planners thinking about shade on everyday routes
cases.use_context: Landscape street-section explainer for public workshops
cases.user_goal: Show how shade, evapotranspiration, surface choice, and street geometry combine at pedestrian height.

content_basis.verified_content: Vegetation cools through shade and evapotranspiration; material properties and building geometry influence heat and airflow.
content_basis.interpretation: The street section is a pedagogical model of exposure, not a computational microclimate simulation.
content_basis.demonstration: Street width, tree spacing, and building dimensions are illustrative and labelled conceptual.

cases.visual_intent: A long street cutaway with tree canopy shadows cast across pedestrians, roof and pavement material bands, and airflow arrows that bend around buildings.

criteria.condition: Shade and evapotranspiration are visually and verbally distinct cooling mechanisms.
criteria.method: Inspect canopy labels, leaf-water glyphs, and ground-shadow treatment.

criteria.condition: Street geometry and surface materials are labelled without unsupported numeric performance claims.
criteria.method: Compare all labels to B04-C05 and inspect the conceptual-model note.

criteria.condition: Pedestrians remain visible, shadows do not obscure annotations, and airflow arrows do not cross body copy.
criteria.method: Review full PNG and local crops at the centre and both ends of the section.

criteria.condition: The diagram makes clear that cooling depends on placement, vegetation, water, and local conditions.
criteria.method: Read the visible limitation line and confirm it is legible at target size.

cases.title: After Sunset, the City Exhales
cases.audience: Readers who assume cooler evenings automatically end heat risk
cases.use_context: Wide editorial timeline, desktop or presentation display
cases.user_goal: Explain slow heat release, warmer nighttime conditions, and why warm nights can matter.

content_basis.verified_content: Urban materials can release stored heat slowly; nighttime heat islands occur; warm overnight lows can sustain heat stress.
content_basis.interpretation: The city 'exhaling' is a metaphor for radiative heat release, not a literal measured flux.
content_basis.demonstration: The time strip is qualitative and contains no invented hourly temperatures.

cases.visual_intent: A dusk-to-dawn ribbon in which a built mass glows and releases upward heat bands; the lower band holds short time-of-day markers rather than a fake data curve.

criteria.condition: The piece explicitly links sunset to continued stored-heat release rather than immediate cooling.
criteria.method: Inspect the headline, central mass, and release arrows.

criteria.condition: No hourly curve or numeric cooling rate is shown without data.
criteria.method: Check the artwork for axes/values and confirm the qualitative-time note is visible.

criteria.condition: Warm-night risk is explained with appropriate limits and not framed as medical advice.
criteria.method: Review the risk annotation against B04-C06 and confirm no treatment advice appears.

criteria.condition: Time markers, heat bands, and captions remain aligned and legible at 16:9.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG and a resized 50% thumbnail.

cases.title: Who Gets the Shade?
cases.audience: Community organizers, equity reviewers, and residents comparing public-space access
cases.use_context: Portrait editorial feature with workshop discussion prompts
cases.user_goal: Frame access to shade and cooling as uneven exposure and access, without inventing demographic statistics.

content_basis.verified_content: EPA links lower vegetation with hotter areas and demographic patterns; heat concern varies with age, income, occupation, health, disability, mobility, and access to cool spaces.
content_basis.interpretation: The route-to-shade comparison is an editorial way to discuss access, not a measured equity index.
content_basis.demonstration: Any two route lengths or shade percentages would be fictional; the plan avoids quantitative route claims.

cases.visual_intent: Two abstract neighbourhood routes converge on one shaded civic destination; one route is exposed and fragmented, the other continuous. Human-scale annotations carry the equity questions.

criteria.condition: The piece distinguishes exposure, access to cool space, and individual vulnerability rather than collapsing them into one label.
criteria.method: Read the three annotation categories and compare with B04-C07.

criteria.condition: No demographic percentage, neighbourhood ranking, or causal claim beyond the sources is displayed.
criteria.method: Inspect all text and metadata; check that no local map or fabricated statistic is present.

criteria.condition: The route metaphor is visibly labelled conceptual and does not imply a real place or measured distance.
criteria.method: Inspect the route legend and demonstration note.

criteria.condition: Human figures and access annotations remain readable and respectful, with no stereotype-based iconography.
criteria.method: Visual review at full size and 50%; inspect annotation crops.

cases.title: What 96°F Feels Like
cases.audience: Readers interpreting heat alerts, outdoor activity plans, or apparent-temperature values
cases.user_goal: Understand the NWS Heat Index example and the assumptions that limit what a feels-like value means.

content_basis.verified_content: NWS worked example: 96°F air temperature and 65% RH produce a 121°F heat index; shade/light-wind assumptions; full sunshine can increase values by up to 15°F; WBGT and HeatRisk include other factors.
content_basis.interpretation: The equation-like layout is explanatory; it does not claim that Heat Index measures every exposure pathway.
content_basis.demonstration: The numbers are a source example, not a forecast, live reading, or fictional city observation.

cases.visual_intent: A bold three-part numeric equation above a layered assumptions card, with small context strips for WBGT and HeatRisk. Heat colour is restrained around the numbers to preserve legibility.

criteria.condition: 96°F, 65% RH, and 121°F appear with correct units and roles, transcribed exactly from the NWS example.
criteria.method: Compare rendered text with B04-D02 and b04_s09.txt line 61.

criteria.condition: Shade/light-wind assumptions and the up-to-15°F full-sunshine caveat are visible and are not turned into a fixed addition.
criteria.method: Read all assumption copy and verify no 136°F derived value appears.

criteria.condition: WBGT and HeatRisk context is accurate and does not imply that Heat Index is a universal risk scale.
criteria.method: Cross-check labels with b04_s09.txt lines 63-89 and inspect visible qualifiers.

criteria.condition: Numbers dominate without hiding caveats; all small text remains readable and uncropped.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG, 50% view, and crops of assumptions and context strips.

cases.title: Four Ways to Cool a Block
cases.audience: Residents and planners comparing practical cooling interventions
cases.use_context: Wide comparison feature for desktop reading and public meetings
cases.user_goal: Compare trees/vegetation, green roofs, cool roofs, and cool pavements by mechanism, best-fit context, maintenance, and co-benefits.

content_basis.verified_content: Source-described mechanisms and tradeoffs for four strategies; EPA says no single policy solution fits every community.
content_basis.interpretation: The comparison axes are an editorial synthesis of source discussions.
content_basis.demonstration: No universal score, fabricated cost, or incomparable effect-size ranking.

cases.visual_intent: Four vertical strategy 'specimen' columns built from architectural sections: canopy, planted roof, reflective roof, and pavement layers. A shared comparison rail makes differences easy to scan.

criteria.condition: All four strategies have accurate mechanism, context, maintenance/feasibility, and co-benefit entries.
criteria.method: Review each column against B04-C10 and its source locators.

criteria.condition: The matrix explicitly avoids a universal winner or aggregate score and notes local-climate dependence.
criteria.method: Inspect the header note and check that no total-score row appears.

criteria.condition: Rows align across four columns and no text wraps into an adjacent column or below its container.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG, 50% thumbnail, and column-boundary crops.

criteria.condition: Architectural specimens remain visually distinct while sharing a coherent visual system.
criteria.method: Full-size visual review and side-by-side column comparison.

cases.title: Draw a Cool Corridor
cases.audience: Community groups and planners discussing how isolated interventions can connect
cases.user_goal: Explore a connected sequence of shade, cooler surfaces, rest points, and measurement rather than one-off projects.

content_basis.verified_content: Mechanisms for shade, cool roofs, and cool pavements; strategy selection depends on climate, co-benefits, funding, vulnerability data, and feasibility.
content_basis.interpretation: A connected cool corridor is the special's editorial proposal for discussion, not a source-endorsed standard.
content_basis.demonstration: All geography, route length, budget, measurements, and stakeholder names are fictional and must be visibly labelled.

cases.visual_intent: An axonometric fictional street corridor with five connected interventions and a bottom planning rail linking each move to a question, owner, and evidence need.

criteria.condition: The artwork visibly says 'Fictional planning demonstration' and every invented quantity is marked demo.
criteria.method: Inspect headline/subtitle, map legend, and any numeric annotation.

criteria.condition: The corridor connects at least three intervention types and includes a measurement/feedback step.
criteria.method: Trace the route and cross-check the bottom planning rail.

criteria.condition: No predicted temperature drop, cost saving, or health outcome is presented as measured fact.
criteria.method: Review all copy and confirm only non-numeric planning claims or visibly demo values.

criteria.condition: Axonometric geometry, route, labels, and planning rail remain readable with no occlusion.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG and crops around building tops, street level, and bottom rail.

cases.title: Measure Before You Map
cases.audience: Community science teams, libraries, schools, and municipal staff starting a heat assessment
cases.use_context: Closing portrait field guide that readers can use as a checklist
cases.user_goal: Turn the special into an actionable, method-aware sequence: ask, choose, measure, document, interpret, and act.

content_basis.verified_content: Define objectives, geography, time/season, air-versus-surface data needs; use representative sites, enough sites, consistent protocols, and metadata.
content_basis.interpretation: The six-step field guide condenses EPA's decision framework and measurement considerations.
content_basis.demonstration: No sample sensor reading is shown as real. Any checklist icon or example route is illustrative.

cases.visual_intent: A vertical field-notebook page with six numbered checkpoints, a small air-versus-surface instrument key, and a final evidence-to-action loop.

criteria.condition: All six steps are present in a logical order and cover objective, place/time, data type, protocol, metadata, and interpretation/action.
criteria.method: Trace the numbered sequence and compare with B04-C12.

criteria.condition: Air and surface measurements are not treated as interchangeable, and satellite limitations are acknowledged.
criteria.method: Inspect instrument key and limitation note against b04_s12.txt lines 100-104.

criteria.condition: No claim is made that a small sensor sample automatically represents the whole city.
criteria.method: Review visible caution copy and absence of extrapolation claims.

criteria.condition: Checklist body text, numerals, instrument labels, and source note are readable without clipping on the portrait page.
criteria.method: Inspect full PNG, 50% thumbnail, and crops of each checklist row.
